title: Bronchiectasis, lung abscess and aspergilloma surgery: diagnosis, surgical resection and cavitary disease
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 57 (Pulmonary Infections and Suppurations)
Shields General Thoracic Surgery 8e Ch 83 (Bronchiectasis and Lung Abscess)
BTS Guideline for Bronchiectasis in Adults

steps.say: Bronchiectasis is irreversible abnormal dilatation of the bronchi resulting from chronic infection and airway wall destruction. Recurrent transmural bacterial infection and intense host inflammation destroy muscular and elastic supporting structures. Patients present with copious purulent daily sputum, chronic productive cough, and recurrent life-threatening hemoptysis.
steps.tx: Clinically, **bronchiectasis** represents permanent, irreversible **bronchial dilatation** driven by a vicious cycle of transmural bronchial infection, impaired mucociliary clearance, and chronic neutrophilic elastase destruction. Patients present with daily copious foul-smelling sputum, recurrent respiratory sepsis, and episodic **massive hemoptysis** from hypertrophied bronchial arteries.

vis.caption: Radiographic and cross-sectional signs of severe suppurative airway dilatation. Credit: StewardMD.
vis.alt: Chest radiograph and computed tomography showing tram-track opacities and bronchial wall thickening.

steps.say: High-resolution computed tomography is the gold standard imaging modality for diagnosing bronchiectasis. The classic finding is the signet ring sign, where the internal bronchial diameter exceeds the diameter of the adjacent pulmonary artery branch. Affected airways also demonstrate lack of normal peripheral bronchial tapering.
steps.tx: Volumetric **high-resolution CT** is the definitive imaging gold standard. It demonstrates the pathognomonic **signet ring sign**, where the internal luminal diameter of a dilated bronchus exceeds the diameter of the accompanying pulmonary artery branch, alongside lack of peripheral **bronchial tapering** and mucosal impaction.

rows: Bronchial internal diameter > adjacent pulmonary artery
Hallmark of cylindrical and varicose bronchiectasis
Airway maintains wide caliber within 1 cm of pleura
Indicates severe destruction of peripheral bronchial cartilage
Parallel thickened bronchial walls running longitudinally
Reflects chronic mucosal edema and peribronchial fibrosis

steps.say: Surgical resection is reserved for localized disease or refractory hemorrhage. When medical management fails, anatomical lobectomy or segmentectomy eradicates the infectious reservoir. Massive hemoptysis refractory to bronchial artery embolization also mandates urgent surgical extirpation.
steps.tx: Surgery is indicated for **localized disease** strictly confined to one or two anatomical segments or a single lobe that fails medical therapy. It also serves as life-saving treatment for massive hemoptysis refractory to **bronchial artery embolization**, with **anatomic lobectomy** providing definitive source control.

nodes.label: Document localized focal bronchiectasis on HRCT
Optimize medical management with chest physiotherapy and targeted antibiotics
Persistent symptoms, localized suppuration, or refractory hemoptysis
Perform anatomic lobectomy or segmentectomy with clear margins

steps.say: Complete surgical resection of all bronchiectatic segments is essential for cure. Leaving dilated, diseased tissue behind guarantees persistent infection and symptoms. The surgeon must achieve clean margins and complete extirpation to prevent recurrent postoperative suppuration.
steps.tx: Achieving **complete extirpation** of all dilated, diseased bronchial segments with **clean margins** is paramount. Leaving residual diseased bronchiectatic segments behind invariably leads to treatment failure and high rates of **recurrent suppuration**, chronic sputum production, and persistent postoperative hemoptysis requiring repeat interventions.

left.title: Complete Anatomical Resection
points: Resects all bronchiectatic segments identified on HRCT
Divided bronchus exhibits healthy mucosal margins
Cures infection and eliminates recurrent hemoptysis

right.title: Incomplete Segmental Clearance
points: Leaves residual dilated bronchial branches behind
Promotes persistent bacterial pooling and chronic sepsis
High rate of recurrent suppuration and secondary bleeding

steps.say: Pulmonary aspergilloma develops within pre-existing cavitary lung lesions. Most cases arise inside old tuberculosis cavities. A fungal ball of hyphae, mucus, and cellular debris forms within the cavity, producing the classic Monod sign or air crescent sign on chest radiography.
steps.tx: A simple **aspergilloma**, or fungal **mycetoma**, consists of a conglomeration of Aspergillus hyphae, fibrin, and cellular debris colonizing a pre-existing lung cavity. On imaging, gravity-dependent movement of the mobile fungal mass produces the characteristic **air crescent sign** or Monod sign.

left.title: Simple Aspergilloma
points: Arises in quiescent pre-existing cavity (old healed TB)
Surrounding lung parenchyma is thin-walled and normal
Lower operative risk during anatomical lobectomy

right.title: Complex Aspergilloma
points: Arises in chronically diseased, destroyed lung parenchyma
Surrounded by dense vascular adhesions and pleural fibrosis
High operative blood loss and risk of bronchopleural fistula

steps.say: Surgical resection is the definitive treatment for symptomatic aspergilloma associated with hemoptysis. Preoperative systemic antifungals lack efficacy in penetrating the non-vascular cavity. Dissection must be meticulous to avoid spillage of fungal contents into the pleural space, which causes severe Aspergillus empyema.
steps.tx: Surgical **cavitary resection** remains the **definitive treatment** of choice for aspergilloma complicated by hemoptysis, because medical antifungals cannot penetrate the avascular fungal ball. Meticulous technique ensuring **fungal spillage avoidance** is vital to prevent fatal pleural cavity contamination and chronic fungal empyema.

nodes.label: Identify mycetoma with air crescent sign in patient with hemoptysis
Perform formal pulmonary function testing and contrast chest CT
Execute careful anatomical lobectomy without tearing cavity wall
Extract specimen intact, avoiding fungal spillage into pleural space

steps.say: Primary lung abscesses most commonly result from aspiration of oral secretions. Aspiration of anaerobic oral flora occurs in patients with impaired consciousness from alcohol or seizure disorders. Targeted prolonged antibiotic therapy succeeds in greater than 85 to 90 percent of cases.
steps.tx: A primary **lung abscess** is typically triggered by **aspiration** of **anaerobic flora** and microaerophilic streptococci in patients with depressed consciousness. First-line therapy with targeted intravenous and oral antibiotics achieves complete clinical and radiographic resolution in over 85 to 90 percent of cases without surgery.

rows: Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin for 4-6 weeks
External catheter decompression of peripheral non-resolving cavity
Excision of necrotic lung and diseased bronchial tree

steps.say: Surgical resection for lung abscess is reserved for medical failure. Indications include lack of clinical improvement after four to six weeks of antibiotics, a large thick-walled cavity exceeding 4 to 6 centimetres, life-threatening hemoptysis, or suspected underlying endobronchial carcinoma.
steps.tx: Surgical intervention is indicated for a **refractory abscess** failing 4 to 6 weeks of antibiotics, a **cavity size** exceeding 4 to 6 cm refractory to drainage, life-threatening hemorrhage, or suspected underlying bronchogenic carcinoma. Standard **surgical resection** via lobectomy provides definitive cure while preventing recurrent sepsis.
